article.title: The World Should Not Ignore China’s Undervalued Currency

metadata_extension.subtitle: A weak renminbi directly led to China’s latest export boom, and a stronger renminbi is the only realistic cure.

summary.central_question: Should the world press China to let its undervalued currency appreciate, or wait for Chinese domestic reforms to rebalance?
summary.main_thesis: China's deeply undervalued currency matters and should not be ignored; appreciation is an effective, needed tool, and waiting for domestic reform alone risks continued inaction and a growing China shock.

content.text: Should the world press China to let its undervalued currency appreciate, or wait for Chinese domestic reforms to rebalance?
content.reason: A large persistent surplus raises the question of which policy lever should be used to correct it.

passages.source_excerpt: argue that the world shouldn’t press China to change how it manages its currency.

content.text: China's reported surplus implies about 20 percent undervaluation by the IMF's own model, and adjusted for gold and investment income, 30-35 percent.
content.reason: An external surplus above its norm signals an undervalued real exchange rate.

passages.source_excerpt: China’s current account surplus is now reported to be around 4 percent of GDP—or 3 percentage points higher than what the IMF estimates it should be. That works out, using the IMF’s own calculations, to an undervaluation of roughly 20 percent.

content.text: China's reported investment income deficit despite large net foreign assets is misreported, so the true surplus is larger.
content.reason: Distrust official figures that cannot be reconciled with known asset positions or independently verified.

passages.source_excerpt: China reports a deficit of $125 billion on $4 trillion in net assets, something that no one—the IMF included—can explain

content.text: Accumulated surpluses should generate net foreign assets that earn positive investment income.
content.reason: Net creditors normally earn net income on their external assets.

passages.source_excerpt: a long history of surpluses should lead to a positive net foreign asset position and thus external investment income (as in Korea, Taiwan, and Japan).

content.text: The PBOC controls the yuan through the daily fix and state-bank FX purchases of about $50 billion a month, under a largely closed financial account.
content.reason: A government that sets the midpoint and intervenes at scale determines its exchange rate.

passages.source_excerpt: The yuan, in other words, goes where the PBOC wants it to go.

content.text: Gopinath, Gourinchas and Rey argue that exchange rate moves matter little, that nominal appreciation would be offset by deflation, and that the world should wait for China to boost domestic demand.
content.reason: Rebut the strongest expert case for inaction.

passages.source_excerpt: Gopinath, Gourinchas, and Rey

content.text: Waiting is costly because China's model depends on an ever-growing surplus, displacing traded-goods production abroad and concentrating industry in China.
content.reason: Growth driven by net exports requires a continually expanding trade surplus.

passages.source_excerpt: the status quo is one where China relies on an increasing surplus to make up for the ongoing weakness of its own internal economy.

content.text: The PBOC allowed the 2022-23 depreciation of 10-15 percent against the dollar, and with Chinese deflation versus Western inflation it became a real depreciation.
content.reason: Under divergent inflation, a nominal depreciation translates nearly fully into a real one.

passages.source_excerpt: That nominal move would not have happened without the tacit support of the PBOC.

reasons: boxes: `E3` the name `western` does not occur in the article

content.text: Productivity catch-up implies a trend real appreciation, so depreciation relative to trend has a bigger effect.
content.reason: Converging economies should see their real exchange rates rise over time.

passages.source_excerpt: China’s convergence in manufacturing productivity with the advanced economies should result in a real appreciation.

content.text: The IMF's standard model predicts a 10 percent currency move shifts net exports by 1.5 pp of GDP.
content.reason: Compare observed outcomes to established elasticity estimates.

passages.source_excerpt: the IMF’s standard exchange rate model suggests a 10 percent move in China’s currency should lead to a 1.5 percentage point increase in net exports

content.text: Chinese exports accelerated 4-5 quarters after the depreciation, with net exports contributing 1.5 pp to growth in 2024 and 2025, matching the model.
content.reason: Outcomes that match a model's lagged prediction support the model.

passages.source_excerpt: That acceleration then shows up as 1.5 pp contribution from net exports to China’s growth in both 2024 and 2025.

content.text: A weaker currency makes exports cheaper and boosts export growth after a lag of a year or more.
content.reason: Trade volumes respond to relative prices with a lag.

passages.source_excerpt: exchange rate changes do matter, and they have their biggest impact with a lag.

content.text: The IMF forecast that China's surplus would shrink, but it grew instead because the forecasts ignored the real depreciation.
content.reason: Forecasts that ignore exchange rate moves will miss the trade adjustment.

passages.source_excerpt: In 2022, 2023, and again in 2024, the IMF’s official forecast for China showed that China’s external surplus would shrink, not rise, over time

content.text: Industrial policy and a domestic market rigged against imports also drove China's export surge.
content.reason: Trade outcomes usually have several contributing causes.

passages.source_excerpt: Is “currency” the entire story of the last few years? No, of course not.

content.text: Nominal appreciation produces real appreciation because domestic prices adjust only partially and slowly.
content.reason: Sticky prices mean nominal exchange rate moves pass into real exchange rates.

passages.source_excerpt: Exchange rates can move quickly; domestic prices adjust partially and with a long lag. There isn’t an immediate offset.

content.text: Empirical work, highlighted by Krugman, and China's recent data show no deflation offset to nominal moves.
content.reason: Long-standing empirical regularities carry weight against theoretical offsets.

passages.source_excerpt: Solid (if old) empirical work has long found that nominal exchange rate moves do result in real exchange rate moves. Krugman highlighted this back in 2011.

content.text: The moderation in China's deflation partly reflects higher oil prices, not only the exchange rate.
content.reason: Acknowledge confounding factors in price data.

passages.source_excerpt: I fully accept that higher oil prices have had something to do with that.

content.text: Xi will not adopt household stimulus without external pressure; an appreciation that removed net-export growth would force such choices.
content.reason: Governments change entrenched policy only when the current strategy stops delivering.

passages.source_excerpt: There is no sign that waiting for President Xi to see the light will lead China to start writing big checks to households any time soon.

content.text: Landau and Jean argue the weak real exchange rate is a deliberate feature of Xi's strategy, supporting industrial upgrading without household transfers.
content.reason: A policy that serves a leader's goals will persist unless those goals are challenged.

passages.source_excerpt: a weak real exchange rate is a core feature of Xi’s China, and not just a by-product of the current cyclical downturn.

content.text: Exchange rate diplomacy has worked: Plaza reduced imbalances without causing Japan's bubble, and China appreciated under pressure in 2007-08 and 2011.
content.reason: Past episodes of coordinated currency adjustment show the tool can work.

passages.source_excerpt: The Plaza Accords, contrary to the arguments made by the G7 economists, did actually bring down the overall U.S. trade deficit as well as Japan’s surplus.

content.text: The view that Plaza caused Japan's bubble is wrong, since Germany appreciated without a bubble and many bubbles have occurred without appreciation.
content.reason: A cause that is neither necessary nor sufficient is a weak explanation.

passages.source_excerpt: the common belief (especially in China) that the Plaza Accords led to Japan’s bubble economy doesn’t stand up to scrutiny.

reasons: passages: `X2`: the team's passage linker anchors it to p46 (shared: plaza), which the box does not cite

content.text: Cutting investment subsidies without raising consumption would enlarge the surplus because the surplus equals savings minus investment.
content.reason: The current account equals national saving minus investment.

passages.source_excerpt: any reduction in investment relative to savings implies a larger surplus

content.text: If the exchange rate is ruled out, closing a surplus of this size would require a fiscal reflation far larger than the IMF's timid 0.5 pp proposal.
content.reason: Rejecting one adjustment tool raises the burden on the remaining tools in proportion to the imbalance.

passages.source_excerpt: If Gopinath, Gourinchas, and Rey don’t believe exchange rate moves have much of an impact and should not be a priority now, the scale of the needed shift to other policies needs to be ramped up

content.text: Households will not anticipate future gains and spend more when inefficient investment is cut.
content.reason: Forward-looking consumption responses are weak in practice.

passages.source_excerpt: Maybe, but I personally wouldn’t bet on it. Cutting inefficient property investment didn’t magically spur household consumption

content.text: The world, led now by Europe, should press China to let the renminbi appreciate, while also pressing for large centrally financed fiscal support for households.
content.reason: When an imbalance harms trading partners, they should press for the adjustment known to work.

passages.source_excerpt: Putting a bit of pressure on China to end its current reliance on net exports for an acceptable pace of growth thus seems like an acceptable risk

content.text: China's deeply undervalued currency matters and should not be ignored; appreciation is an effective, needed tool, and waiting for domestic reform alone risks continued inaction and a growing China shock.
content.reason: A proven, fast-acting policy lever should be used rather than waiting on uncertain structural reform.

passages.source_excerpt: And if not exchange rate adjustment—a policy change that is known to work—then what?

content.text: The IMF's standard playbook struggles with a high-saving, state-guided economy, which partly excuses its confused recommendations.
content.reason: Standard models may mislead for economies with unusual structures.

passages.source_excerpt: I do have some sympathy for the IMF here. China is both big, and extremely unbalanced.

content.text: The author agrees that raising household income share and social insurance is needed, and that the property crisis weighs on consumption; he concedes those fundamentals matter too.
content.reason: Concede shared ground before disputing priorities.

passages.source_excerpt: No disagreement from me. I would add that China also needs to change its very regressive system of taxation.
